title: Toxidromes & High-Yield Overdoses
sources: Critical Vector — EM Pocket Guide: Toxidromes + Specific Overdoses
ACEP toxicology guidance; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; regional poison-center protocols

changelog.change: Initial entry — the toxidrome recognition table + serotonin-syndrome/NMS, and the highest-yield specific-overdose regimens (APAP, TCA, BB/CCB, sympathomimetic, salicylate). Full antidote dosing lives in the antidotes-reversal-agents module.

summary: Read the vitals + pupils + skin together to name the toxidrome, then treat the mechanism. Anticholinergic = hot/dry/flushed, mydriasis, tachycardia. Cholinergic = wet (SLUDGE), miosis, bradycardia. Sympathomimetic = diaphoretic, mydriasis, tachy-hypertensive. Opioid = pinpoint pupils + hypoventilation.

rows: Benzodiazepines for agitation; physostigmine 1–2 mg IV slow ONLY if no QRS widening / TCA cardiotoxicity
Organophosphates, nerve agents, pilocarpine, some mushrooms
Atropine 2–4 mg IV, DOUBLE q5 min, titrate to DRY secretions (not to pupils); pralidoxime 1–2 g IV before the enzyme ages
Naloxone 0.04–0.4 mg IV/IM/IN, titrate to respiration; infusion at ~2/3 the effective waking dose per hour for long-acting opioids
Benzodiazepines first-line; active cooling for hyperthermia; AVOID a pure beta-blocker (unopposed alpha)
Supportive; intubate for airway compromise; flumazenil rarely used (seizure risk)
SSRI/SNRI, MAOI, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, fentanyl, methylene blue
Stop the agent(s); benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine 12 mg PO load then 2 mg q2h; active cooling; onset over HOURS
Antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine); also abrupt dopamine-agonist withdrawal
Stop the antipsychotic; benzodiazepines; bromocriptine 2.5 mg q8h ± dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV; cooling; onset over DAYS

body.text: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS: tempo and tone. Serotonin syndrome develops over hours with hyperreflexia + clonus (neuromuscular hyperactivity); NMS develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity + sluggish reflexes (hypoactivity).

items: Draw a level at 4 h post-ingestion → plot on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram (a line drawn only for single acute ingestions with a known time).
IV N-acetylcysteine (3-bag): 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Nearly 100% hepatoprotective if started within 8 h.
Unknown time or > 8 h post-ingestion: start NAC empirically now, adjust once the level and timing are known.
Massive ingestion (> 150 mg/kg, level well above the line, or 4-h level > 300): consider a higher NAC loading dose and involve hepatology / toxicology early; fomepizole is an emerging adjunct.

body.text: QRS > 100 ms = high risk of a ventricular arrhythmia; > 160 ms = very high risk; an R wave in aVR > 3 mm is also a high-risk sign. Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg IV bolus (then an infusion), target pH 7.50–7.55 — for hypotension, QRS > 100 ms, arrhythmia, or seizure. Treat the QRS, not the pH. AVOID flumazenil (lowers the seizure threshold), physostigmine, and class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics.

items: Calcium: CaCl₂ 1 g IV q10 min ×3 via central line (or calcium gluconate 3 g peripherally) — best for CCB.
High-dose insulin euglycaemia (HIE): regular insulin ~1 U/kg bolus → 1–10 U/kg/hr, with a concentrated dextrose infusion and frequent glucose / K⁺ checks. Increasingly first-line, not a last resort.
Glucagon 2–5 mg IV bolus → 1–10 mg/hr infusion — beta-blocker-specific (bypasses the blocked receptor). Often under-dosed.

Lipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus for a lipophilic agent (e.g. verapamil, propranolol) refractory to the above. Atropine, pressors, transvenous pacing, and VA-ECMO for refractory shock. Full detail in the antidotes module.

body.text: Tinnitus, tachypnoea, a MIXED respiratory alkalosis + high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia. Serum salicylate level + serial ABG/VBG. Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise the urine (target urine pH 7.5–8) and keep serum pH ~ 7.45–7.55 — this traps salicylate out of the CNS. Glucose even if serum glucose is normal (CNS neuroglycopenia). Haemodialysis for a level > 90–100 mg/dL (acute), altered mentation, pulmonary/cerebral oedema, renal failure, or refractory acidosis. NEVER intubate casually — apnoea during the procedure drops the pH and can precipitate arrest; if you must, match the pre-intubation minute ventilation and pre-treat with bicarbonate.
